newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. envoy discusses Brcko with Bosnian leaders.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy discusses Brcko with Bosnian leaders.

text.p: U.S. envoy John Kornblum held talks with Bosnian Moslem and Serb leaders on Sunday about a volatile territorial dispute over the town of Brcko, U.S. officials and local media reported.
Kornblum, U.S. assistant secretary of state, visited Sarajevo two weeks before a deadline expires for an arbitration process which is supposed to settle Brcko's future status.
The dispute over the narrow Brcko land corridor, which links eastern and western halves of Bosnian Serb-controlled territory, nearly caused peace talks to collapse in November 1995.
Bosnian state radio said Kornblum met Alija Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, and Brcko was among the subjects discussed.

He then drove to the village of Pale, outside Sarajevo, to meet the Serb member of the presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, U.S. embassy officials said. He was also expected to meet Biljana Plavsic, president of the autonomous Serb republic in Bosnia.

A deadline for settling the Brcko dispute has been extended from mid-December to February 15. Serb and Moslem delegations presented their arguments during 10 days of arbitration hearings in Rome last month.

The Bosnian Serbs, who seized Brcko early in the 1992-95 war, insist that the town must be kept under Serb control or Serb territory would be cut in half. They have threatened to go to war over the issue.
Moslem leaders say Brcko should be awarded to the Moslem- Croat federation based on the pre-war population in which Moslems and Croats formed a majority.
They say giving the Sava river port to the Serbs would reward ethnic expulsions carried out when Serb forces captured the area in May 1992.

The U.S. lawyer chairing the arbitration panel, Roberts Owen, is charged with delivering the final verdict but diplomats say Washington and other major powers will have a say before any decision is announced.
A U.S. internal policy paper suggested giving Brcko to the Serbs while allowing the federation a transit route through the area and requiring guarantees for the return of Moslem and Croat refugees.
The State Department denied the paper proposed allowing the Serbs to keep Brcko, but it outraged officials in the Moslem-Croat federation who accused the West of preparing to reward ethnic cleansing.
Diplomats say major powers are also considering some sort of international administration of Brcko to secure the return of refugees and defuse lingering hostility from the war.
Ejup Ganic, former vice-president of the Moslem-Croat federation, told state radio he was more optimistic about the outcome of the dispute after talks with U.S. officials in Washington.
"Now that I have returned from the United States I can tell you we are closer to justice," he said.
